clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive deficiency of coagulation factor X, one of the more severe of the rare inherited bleeding disorders.
Because factor X sits at the start of the common pathway, deficiency prolongs both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time.
Severity broadly tracks the factor X level; severely affected patients can present in the neonatal period with umbilical stump bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage.
Typical manifestations include mucocutaneous bleeding, haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas, menorrhagia and haematuria.
The Russell viper venom time is abnormal, reflecting direct factor X activation, and a specific factor X assay confirms the diagnosis.
Acquired factor X deficiency is classically associated with systemic AL amyloidosis, where factor X is adsorbed onto amyloid fibrils.
Vitamin K deficiency, warfarin and severe liver disease reduce factor X along with the other vitamin K-dependent factors.
Treatment uses factor X or prothrombin complex concentrate; antifibrinolytics assist with mucosal bleeding, and regular prophylaxis may be needed in severe disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Factor X is a vitamin K-dependent serine protease zymogen that occupies the pivotal junction of the coagulation cascade. Activated factor X, in complex with activated factor V, calcium and phospholipid, forms the prothrombinase complex that converts prothrombin to thrombin, the central effector of clot formation. Factor X can be activated either by the extrinsic tissue-factor/factor VIIa pathway or by the intrinsic factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex, which is why its deficiency lengthens both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time. Inherited deficiency results from mutations in the F10 gene and may reduce factor X quantity (type I) or produce a dysfunctional molecule with reduced activity relative to antigen (type II); the resulting fall in thrombin generation impairs both fibrin formation and platelet activation, giving a bleeding tendency that generally parallels the residual activity. Acquired deficiency most characteristically occurs in systemic AL amyloidosis, where factor X binds avidly to amyloid fibrils, particularly in the liver and spleen, and is cleared from the circulation; it also falls, along with factors II, VII and IX, in vitamin K deficiency, vitamin K antagonist therapy and hepatocellular failure.
additionalDifferentials: Factor V deficiency and combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency
Factor VII deficiency (prolonged PT with normal APTT)
Vitamin K deficiency or vitamin K antagonist effect
Liver disease with reduced synthesis of clotting factors
Systemic AL amyloidosis causing acquired factor X deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (both prolonged)
Specific factor X coagulant and antigen assays to define type I versus type II
Mixing studies to distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor
Assays of other vitamin K-dependent factors to exclude combined or acquired causes
Investigations for amyloidosis where acquired deficiency is suspected
F10 genetic analysis and family studies
redFlags: Neonatal umbilical stump bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage
Spontaneous central nervous system or gastrointestinal bleeding
Recurrent haemarthroses or large muscle haematomas causing compartment compromise
Severe menorrhagia or postpartum haemorrhage with anaemia
Features of amyloidosis (nephrotic syndrome, cardiac failure, neuropathy) with new bleeding
reference.prognosis: With modern factor replacement and, where indicated, prophylaxis, severely affected patients can be protected from the most dangerous bleeds and achieve a good quality of life. Prognosis in acquired disease is largely governed by the underlying condition, being particularly guarded when due to systemic amyloidosis.
pitfalls: Overlooking underlying AL amyloidosis when factor X deficiency is acquired rather than inherited
Attributing the combined PT and APTT prolongation to heparin or a global coagulopathy without a specific factor assay
Underestimating neonatal risk in severe deficiency and delaying prophylaxis
Failing to distinguish type I from type II deficiency, which affects antigen-based interpretation
Assuming prothrombin complex concentrate fully corrects deficiency without monitoring the response
references: United Kingdom Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation guidance on rare bleeding disorders (standard reference)
